title: Rule out the prerequisite first
statement: Before reading a failed check as a gap in its content, rule out the prerequisite it leans on, such as decoding for reading comprehension or fluency for math.
example: One math design cites a programme figure that about 25% of math non-growth traces to a lack of fluency.
detail: The RAND Reading Study Group's 2002 report, in a reading course's digest of it, says assessments of young children's reading must control for the level of decoding to assess comprehension adequately (p. 114), and names word-level skills as the primary source of variability in comprehension among beginning and elementary readers; the digest adds that young readers' scores are otherwise confounded with decoding (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/reading-science/DIGEST-rand-mr1465-2002.qmd`, lines 723-725). A grade 4 and 5 math checkpoint design applies the same logic, calling it the math analogue of the reading course's decoding caveat: a checkpoint that fails a non-fluent student and routes them to content misdiagnoses the problem, so checkpoints verify the fluency prerequisite first and route those students out (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g4g5-math-checkpoints/brainlifts/v0.1.md`, line 35). Its 25% figure is relayed from a programme recap, not measured in the design.
against: A grade 1 reading design keeps decoding inside its scored tests, with no text-to-speech on passages or answer choices, since these are reading tests, not listening comprehension tests (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g1-reading/brainlifts/v0.1.md`, line 43).

evidence.quote: must control for the level of decoding to assess comprehension adequately.

Assessments of young children's reading must control for the child's level of word-reading/decoding in order to assess comprehension adequately, since young readers' scores are otherwise confounded with decoding ability.
reader differences in the acquisition of word-level skills are the primary source of variability in reading comprehension in beginning and elementary school–age readers

~25% of math non-growth traces to fluency; *"lack of fluency doubles the time to master a course."* A checkpoint that fails a non-fluent student and routes them to *content* mis-diagnoses the problem.
Checkpoints verify FastMath prerequisite status first and route fluency-gated students out — the math analogue of G1 reading's decoding caveat.

citations.ref: RAND Reading Study Group 2002, Reading for Understanding (MR-1465)
